title: From humans to model organisms: Translational insights into sociability and social dysfunction
title_zh: 从人类到模型生物：关于社会性与社会功能障碍的转化洞察
abstract: Sociability is an evolutionarily conserved biological trait that promotes information exchange, protection, cooperation, and reproductive success. Its expression nevertheless differs substantially across species, from aggregation and social recognition to affiliation, cooperation, and higher-order social cognition. This review establishes a comparative, component-based framework for evaluating what different model organisms can and cannot reveal about human sociability and social dysfunction. We compare social-cue detection, recognition and memory, motivation and reward, contextual integration, and behavioral output across humans, non-human primates, rodents, sheep, zebrafish, frogs, Drosophila, bees, and Caenorhabditis elegans. Humans provide the reference framework, integrating conserved social processes with higher-order capacities such as empathy and Theory of Mind. Autism spectrum disorder is considered as an important translational example of how alterations across partially separable social components can produce heterogeneous phenotypes. Non-human primates permit investigation of social attention, gaze, affiliation, reciprocity, and social reward within neural systems broadly homologous to those of humans. Rodents enable genetic and circuit-level analysis of social approach, recognition, memory, bonding, and parental behavior, whereas sheep support ethologically grounded studies of individual recognition, maternal-offspring bonding, and group cohesion. Zebrafish and frogs provide complementary access to the development and sensory organization of vertebrate social behavior. Drosophila, bees, and C. elegans offer genetic precision for investigating aggregation, communication, social organization, and conserved molecular mechanisms. No single species reproduces the full complexity of human sociability or a complete clinical disorder. Instead, each provides experimental access to particular social components and mechanisms, with distinct strengths and interpretive limitations. Integrating findings across complementary models can therefore clarify the biological organization of sociability and strengthen translation to human social dysfunction.
abstract_zh: 社会性是一种进化上保守的生物特征，促进信息交流、保护、合作和繁殖成功。然而，其表达在不同物种之间差异显著，从聚集和社会识别到亲属关系、合作以及更高级的社会认知。本综述建立了一个比较、基于组成部分的框架，用以评估不同模型生物能否揭示人类社会性和社会功能障碍的哪些方面。我们比较了人类、非人灵长类、啮齿类、绵羊、斑马鱼、青蛙、果蝇、蜜蜂和秀丽隐杆线虫在社会线索检测、识别与记忆、动机与奖励、情境整合以及行为输出方面的差异。人类提供了参考框架，将保守的社会过程与更高级的能力（如共情和心智理论）相结合。自闭症谱系障碍被视为一个重要的转化示例，说明部分可分离的社会组成部分的改变如何产生异质性表型。非人灵长类动物允许在与人类高度同源的神经系统中研究社会注意、凝视、亲属关系、互惠和社会奖励。啮齿类动物则支持对社会接近、识别、记忆、结合和亲代行为的遗传和回路层面分析，而绵羊支持基于生态学的个体识别、母子结合和群体凝聚力研究。斑马鱼和青蛙提供了对脊椎动物社会行为发育和感官组织的互补性研究途径。果蝇、蜜蜂和秀丽隐杆线虫则提供了遗传精度，用于研究聚集、通信、社会组织和保守的分子机制。没有单一物种能再现人类社会性的全部复杂性或完整的临床障碍。相反，每种物种都提供了对特定社会组成部分和机制的实验通道，具有各自的优势和解释局限性。因此，整合互补模型的发现可以阐明社会性的生物学组织，并加强对人类社会功能障碍的转化。
